decision.retrieved_from: Alabama Supreme Court opinion PDF via CourtListener cluster 10847586
decision.ai_tool_found: generative AI, tool unidentified; at the show-cause hearing counsel (Hall) “admitted that many of the legal authorities in his briefs do not exist and that he improperly used AI to obtain those authorities”
decision.note: Passages in quotation marks within the opinion's Part II.A are the court's verbatim quotation of the appellee's brief, adopted by the court as its account of the fabrications.

offending.as_cited: Ex parte Helms, 873 So. 2d 1139 (Ala. 2003)
offending.court_quote: First, Appellants cite to Ex parte Helms, 873 So. 2d 1139 (Ala. 2003). Helms does not involve a trust or Ala. Code § 19-3B-604(a). … Notably, Appellants provide a quotation from Helms that is not present anywhere in the Helms opinion.
offending.what_actually_exists: Ex parte Helms, 873 So. 2d 1139 (Ala. 2003) is real: a will-contest case holding that testamentary capacity could be found even where a person was not competent to transact ordinary, everyday affairs (873 So. 2d at 1147). It involves no trust and not § 19-3B-604(a).

offending.as_cited: Janowiak v. Tiesi, 932 N.E.2d 569, 577 (Ill. App. Ct. 2010)
offending.court_quote: Appellants next provide a quotation that is not found in Janowiak v. Tiesi, 932 N.E.2d 569, 577 (Ill. App. Ct. 2010), a case that actually involves a trust but never discusses a trust instrument's legal validity or a contest thereof.
offending.what_actually_exists: Janowiak v. Tiesi, 932 N.E.2d 569 (Ill. App. Ct. 2010) is real and involves a trust, but never discusses a trust instrument's legal validity or a contest of one.

offending.as_cited: In re Estate of McFarland, 167 S.W.3d 299 (Tenn. 2005)
offending.court_quote: Appellants additionally support their argument by citing to In re Estate of McFarland, 167 S.W.3d 299 (Tenn. 2005), which Appellants also misquote regarding trust contests. … Indeed, McFarland has nothing to do with trust validity, but rather is a Tennessee Supreme Court case regarding the construction of a last will and testament and Tennessee's anti-lapse statute.
offending.what_actually_exists: In re Estate of McFarland, 167 S.W.3d 299 (Tenn. 2005) is real and concerns construction of a will and Tennessee's anti-lapse statute.

offending.as_cited: In re Trust of Eickhoff, 974 N.W.2d 505, 514 (Neb. Ct. App. 2022)
offending.court_quote: Most striking, however, is that Appellants next cite to, and provide purported quotations from, an out-of-state case which does not appear to exist. Appellants' provided citation of ‘In re Trust of Eickhoff, 974 N.W.2d 505, 514 (Neb. Ct. App. 2022)’, alleged to be an on-point case from the Nebraska Court of Appeals, is actually one of two Iowa criminal court cases before the Iowa Supreme Court.

offending.as_cited: Ex parte Seabol, 782 So. 2d 212, 216 (Ala. 2000)
offending.quoted_text: [a] fiduciary relationship imposes an obligation to disclose material facts, and failure to do so may constitute fraudulent concealment sufficient to toll the statute of limitations.
offending.court_quote: Appellants first cite Ex parte Seabol, 782 So. 2d 212, 216 (Ala. 2000) for the proposition that ‘[a] fiduciary relationship imposes an obligation to disclose material facts, and failure to do so may constitute fraudulent concealment sufficient to toll the statute of limitations.’ … the quotation attributed to this case is erroneous and the quoted language does not exist on the cited page or anywhere else in the opinion.
offending.what_actually_exists: Ex parte Seabol, 782 So. 2d 212 (Ala. 2000) is a real Alabama Supreme Court decision; the quoted language appears nowhere in it.

offending.as_cited: McGowan v. Chrysler Corp., 631 So. 2d 842, 845 (Ala. 1993)

offending.court_quote: Appellants thereafter quote McGowan v. Chrysler Corp., 631 So. 2d 842, 845 (Ala. 1993) as stating, ‘Active concealment of facts, when there is a duty to disclose, tolls the running of limitations.’ Again, the quoted language does not exist anywhere in the opinion …
offending.what_actually_exists: McGowan v. Chrysler Corp., 631 So. 2d 842 (Ala. 1993) is real; the quoted language appears nowhere in it.

offending.as_cited: Auto-Owners Ins. Co. v. Abston, 822 So. 2d 1187, 1194 (Ala. 2001)
offending.quoted_text: [W]hen the evidence supports more than one inference as to when the plaintiff discovered or should have discovered the fraud, the question is one for the jury.
offending.court_quote: Not only does the quoted language not exist in the opinion, but Abston materially supports Bruce's argument, as the case involved this Court holding that the statute of limitations on a plaintiff's fraud claim had run as a matter of law, and that it was error for the trial court to have submitted the claim to a jury. 822 So. 2d at 1198.
offending.what_actually_exists: Auto-Owners Ins. Co. v. Abston, 822 So. 2d 1187 (Ala. 2001) is real and holds the opposite: the limitations period had run as a matter of law and it was error to submit the claim to a jury. The real opinion states the period began to run “when the plaintiff was privy to facts which would provoke inquiry in the mind of a [person] of reasonable prudence …” (id. at 1195).

offending.as_cited: Ex parte United Serv. Auto. Ass'n, 78 So. 3d 979, 983-84 (Ala. 2011)
offending.cited_case_name: Ex parte United Serv. Auto. Ass'n
offending.filing: Plaintiffs' reply brief at 17, 27 n.1 and 30
offending.court_quote: Hall cites “Ex parte United Serv. Auto. Ass'n, 78 So. 3d 979”; no such case exists. A case with a nearly identical style — Ex parte United Servs. Auto Ass'n, 365 S.C. 50, 614 S.E. 2d 652 (2005) — is from the South Carolina Court of Appeals and deals with underinsured-motorist benefits. The case assigned that citation is P.A. v. L.S., 78 So. 3d 979 (Ala. Civ. App. 2011), a case dealing with a custody dispute between a mother and paternal grandparents.
offending.what_actually_exists: P.A. v. L.S., 78 So. 3d 979 (Ala. Civ. App. 2011) occupies the cited reporter reference (a custody dispute). A nearly identically styled real case, Ex parte United Servs. Auto Ass'n, 365 S.C. 50, 614 S.E.2d 652 (2005), is a South Carolina underinsured-motorist decision.
